rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Umm literally means the woman who gave birth to you; applying it to grandmothers is literal if the word is shared or polysemous, figurative if not, otherwise their prohibition comes from consensus or another text.
rows.anchor: ولفظ الأم حقيقة في التي ولدتك نفسه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mothers and daughters have been forbidden since Adam; intercourse is degrading, so mothers are protected from it in return for their immense beneficence to children.
rows.anchor: وحرمة الأمهات والبنات كانت من زمان آدم عليه السلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A prohibited daughter is any female descended from you through birth at any degree; whether a granddaughter is literally or figuratively a daughter parallels the grandmother question.
rows.anchor: كل أنثى رجع نسبها إليك بالولادة بدرجة أو درجات

rows.speaker: النضر بن شميل
rows.claim: Al-Naḍr ibn Shumayl records that pre-Islamic Ḥājib ibn Zurārah married his daughter and became a Magian.
rows.anchor: ذكر ذلك: النضر بن شميل في كتاب المثالب.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A prohibited sister is anyone sharing with you a paternal backbone or womb; paternal and maternal aunts mean the father's and mother's sisters.
rows.anchor: الأخت المحرمة كل من جمعك وإياها صلب أو بطن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The text names aunts but not their daughters; grand-aunts are also prohibited, with some collateral aunt relations allowed when they are unrelated to the brother's descendants.
rows.anchor: وخص تحريم العمات والخالات دون أولادهن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nieces remain prohibited however far they descend; singular brother and sister are used because a plural follows, while the singular conveys the whole gendered class.
rows.anchor: وبنات الأخ وبنات الأخت تحرم بناتهما وإن سفلن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Seven women are permanently forbidden by lineage: mother and daughter through birth, plus sister, aunt, and brother's or sister's daughter through sibling relations.
rows.anchor: فهؤلاء سبع من النسب تحريمهن مؤبد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse names nursing mothers and sisters to treat milk kinship like lineage: it gives one example from each of the birth and sibling categories to indicate the rest.
rows.anchor: نبه بذلك على إجراء الرضاع مجرى النسب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophetic rule that nursing forbids what lineage forbids confirms the analogy indicated by the verse.
rows.anchor: يحرم من الرضاع ما يحرم من النسب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Milk kinship maps through the wet nurse and her husband: his parents are grandparents, his sister an aunt, his other children paternal siblings, and her children by him full siblings.
rows.anchor: فزوج المرضعة أبوه، وأبواه جداه، وأخته عمته.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Two exceptions to the nursing rule are marrying one's nursing son's sister or nursing brother's mother, since the intercourse that creates the corresponding lineage bar is absent.
rows.anchor: تحريم الرضاع كتحريم النسب إلا في مسألتين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse does not settle nursing age, number of feeds, milk-father, or ways of administering milk into the stomach; jurists disagree on these matters.
rows.anchor: ولا عدد الرضعات. ولا للبن الفحل، ولا لإرضاع الرجل لبن نفسه للصبي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most read اللاتي أرضعنكم; ʿAbd Allāh reads اللاي, Ibn Hurmuz التي, and Abū Ḥaywah reads الرضاعة with a kasra on rāʾ.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: اللاتي أرضعنكم. وقرأ عبد الله: اللاي بالياء.

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: Most authorities take mothers of wives as an unrestricted prohibition, whether or not the marriage to the daughter was consummated.
rows.anchor: وأمهات نسائكم الجمهور على أنها على العموم. فسواء عقد عليها ولم يدخل

rows.speaker: علي ومجاهد
rows.claim: ʿAlī, Mujāhid, and others allow marrying a wife's mother if the wife was divorced before consummation, treating her like a stepdaughter.
rows.anchor: وروي عن علي ومجاهد وغيرهما: أنه إذا طلقها قبل الدخول، فله أن يتزوج أمها

rows.speaker: علي وداود وأهل الظاهر
rows.claim: They read “stepdaughters in your care” as a condition: if the daughter was not in his care, a man who consummated with her mother may marry her; both custody and consummation must be present for prohibition.
rows.anchor: وإلى هذا ذهب علي، وبه أخذ داود وأهل الظاهر.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Wives of your sons” refers to wives; merely purchasing a slave woman does not bar her to the buyer's father or son, but touching or kissing her does, while lustful looking is disputed.
rows.anchor: وظاهر قوله: وحلائل أبنائكم اختصاص ذلك بالزوجات كما ذكرناه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prohibition on combining two sisters is syntactically coordinated with a raised expression and, in this marriage context, means marrying them together, though the phrase could also include ownership.
rows.anchor: في موضع رفع لعطفه على مرفوع، والمعنى:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The community agrees that a marriage contract combining sisters is forbidden, whether the two contracts occur together or one after the other.
rows.anchor: فأجمعت الأمة على تحريم العقد على ذلك سواء وقع العقدان معا

rows.speaker: زيد وابن عباس وعبيدة وعطاء وابن سيرين ومجاهد
rows.claim: They prohibit marrying a woman during her sister's waiting period; some apply this to any waiting period, others only to a revocable divorce. The author says the apparent verse permits it after an irrevocable divorce.
rows.anchor: فروي عن زيد، وابن عباس، وعبيدة، وعطاء، وابن سيرين، ومجاهد في آخرين

rows.speaker: عروة والقاسم وخلاس
rows.claim: They permit the second marriage when the sister's divorce is irrevocable; this is also the position of Mālik, al-Awzāʿī, al-Layth, and al-Shāfiʿī.
rows.anchor: وروي عن عروة، والقاسم، وخلاس: أنه يجوز له ذلك إذا كانت من طلاق بائن

rows.speaker: عمر وعلي وابن مسعود والزبير وابن عمر وعمار وزيد
rows.claim: These Companions forbid intercourse with two owned sisters; most scholars call it disliked, while Isḥāq calls it forbidden.
rows.anchor: فذهب عمر، وعلي، وابن مسعود، والزبير، وابن عمر، وعمار وزيد: إلى أنه لا يجوز

rows.speaker: أبو العباس أحمد بن علي بن خالص الإشبيلي
rows.claim: Asked by the Hafsid ruler about intercourse with two enslaved sisters, the Tunisian scholar answered that it was prohibited; another authority had permitted it.
rows.anchor: أبو العباس أحمد بن علي بن خالص الإشبيلي: ألا ترى عن الجمع بين الأختين بملك اليمين في الوطء؟ فأجابه بالمنع،

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One interpretation takes the protected women as wives and the exception as enslaved women acquired by transfer of ownership, since the owner's right to sexual access supersedes the prior husband's.
rows.anchor: وقيل: المحصنات المزوجات، والمستثنى هن الإماء، فتحرم المزوجات

rows.speaker: عبد الله وأبي جابر وابن عباس وسعيد والحسن
rows.claim: They hold that enslaved women acquired through purchase, gift, charity, or inheritance are excepted from the ban on married women.
rows.anchor: وإلى هذا ذهب عبد الله، وأبي جابر، وابن عباس أيضا، وسعيد، والحسن.

rows.speaker: عمرو بن عباس وأبو العالية وعبيدة وطاووس وابن جبير وعطاء
rows.claim: They understand the protected women as chaste women generally and the exception as marriage or ownership, making the passage a prohibition of fornication.
rows.anchor: وذهب عمرو بن عباس أيضا، وأبو العالية، وعبيدة، وطاووس، وابن جبير، وعطاء: إلى أن المحصنات هن العفائف

rows.speaker: عمر
rows.claim: A report from ʿUmar identifies the protected women as free women; the exception then means marriage if connected, or enslaved women if disconnected.
rows.anchor: وروي عن عمر في المحصنات أنهن الحرائر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Iḥṣān can encompass its four shared senses; Quranic and Prophetic usage of “what your right hands possess” means enslaved women, and the exception applies to valid forms of protection, including a captive or married slave woman.
rows.anchor: والذي يقتضيه لفظ الإحصان إن تعلق بالقدر المشترك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The seven canonical readers all use fatḥa on ṣād in this phrase; al-Kisāʾī uses kasra in other occurrences, others and ʿAlqamah use fatḥa, and Yazīd ibn Qutayb uses ḍamma by assimilation.
rows.anchor: ولم يختلف القراء السبعة في فتح الصاد من قوله

rows.speaker: مكي
rows.claim: Makkī says “of women” specifies the intended sex, since “those who slander the protected” might otherwise include men, although the community agrees the Quranic penalty applies to slandering a man too.
rows.anchor: وقال مكي: فائدة قوله: من النساء، أن المحصنات تقع على الأنفس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An anonymous poetic line depicts a married captive taken by force as lawful to a new husband despite not being divorced, illustrating the captive-wife interpretation.
rows.anchor: وذات حليل أنكحتها رماحنا ... حلال لمن يبني بها لم تطلق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “What is beyond that” generally permits other women; the author rejects the strained interpretation by ʿUbaydah and al-Suddī that it means fewer than five wives, and notes al-Suddī's alternative of sex short of penetration.
rows.anchor: وأبعد عبيدة والسدي في رد ذلك إلى مثنى وثلاث ورباع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: General permission is qualified by the established Sunna forbidding a man to combine a woman with her paternal or maternal aunt; it otherwise includes marriage to female cousins.
rows.anchor: والظاهر العموم إلا ما خصته السنة المستفيضة من تحريم الجمع

rows.speaker: إسحاق بن طلحة وعكرمة وقتادة وعطاء
rows.claim: They reportedly prohibit some cousin combinations; Ḥasan ibn Ḥusayn nevertheless married two paternal cousins in one night, and Mālik disliked but did not forbid it.
rows.anchor: وقد روي المنع من ذلك عن: إسحاق بن طلحة، وعكرمة، وقتادة، وعطاء.

rows.speaker: ابن المنذر
rows.claim: Ibn al-Mundhir knows no scholar who invalidated marriage to two cousins together, since neither scripture, Sunna, nor consensus excludes them from the general permission.
rows.anchor: قال ابن المنذر: لا أعلم أحدا، أبطل هذا النكاح

rows.speaker: أكثر أهل العلم
rows.claim: Most scholars hold that fornication does not bar later marriage to the woman, her mother, or daughter, and does not make one's wife forbidden after sex with her mother or daughter.
rows.anchor: وعلى هذا أكثر أهل العلم

rows.speaker: عمران بن حصين والشعبي وعطاء والحسن وسفيان وأحمد وإسحاق
rows.claim: They, along with Abū Ḥanīfah, hold that fornication with a woman bars marriage to her mother and daughter, contrary to the majority.
rows.anchor: وروي عن عمران بن حصين والشعبي، وعطاء، والحسن، وسفيان، وأحمد، وإسحاق، أنهما يحرمان عليه

rows.speaker: مالك وأبو حنيفة والشافعي وأصحابه
rows.claim: They say sexual abuse of a male does not bar marriage to his mother or daughter; al-Thawrī and ʿUbayd Allāh ibn al-Ḥasan analogize it to intercourse, while al-Awzāʿī bars the offender from marrying a daughter born to the victim.
rows.anchor: وبه قال: مالك وأبو حنيفة والشافعي وأصحابه قالوا: لا يحرم النكاح العبث بالرجال.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥamzah, al-Kisāʾī, and Ḥafṣ read “was made lawful” passively; the other canonical readers read it actively with God as subject. Both readings coordinate with “forbidden to you.”
rows.anchor: ولا فرق في العطف بين أن يكون الفعل مبنيا للفاعل، أو للمفعول.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī coordinates the active reading with an implied “God prescribed,” but the author rejects the distinction: “God's book” emphatically reinforces the prohibition, so permission and prohibition clauses are parallel.
rows.anchor: وما اختاره من التفرقة غير مختار

rows.speaker: ابن عطية والفراء والزجاج
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyyah glosses “beyond” as what follows consideration of the prohibited, al-Farrāʾ as everything besides it, and al-Zajjāj as what comes after it; the explanations are close.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عطية: والوراء في هذه الآية ما يعتبر أمره بعد اعتبار المحرمات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The infinitive “that you seek” is an appositional specification of “what is beyond that”; seeking with wealth can mean marriage or purchase, though another view limits it to marriage.
rows.anchor: وموضع أن تبتغوا نصب على أنه بدل اشتمال من ما وراء ذلكم

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī reads “that you seek” as a purpose clause: God clarified lawful and forbidden relations so people would spend wealth on marriage while chaste, avoiding worldly and religious loss.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: أن تبتغوا مفعول له، بمعنى: بين لكم ما يحل مما يحرم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author criticizes al-Zamakhsharī's ornate paraphrase and hidden Muʿtazilī premise, including added words and restricting divine will to marriage; the verse straightforwardly permits pursuing what lies beyond the prohibitions with wealth in chastity.
rows.anchor: وظاهر الآية غير هذا الذي فهمه الزمخشري

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The purpose-clause reading lacks the required shared agent: God is the subject of “made lawful,” while the addressees seek; al-Zamakhsharī inserts an unexpressed intention to align them, unnecessarily departing from the apparent syntax.
rows.anchor: لأنه فات شرط من شروط المفعول له، وهو اتحاد الفاعل في العامل والمفعول له.

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī suggests the omitted object of “seek” is women, or preferably leaves it unstated and paraphrases the phrase as spending wealth.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: (فإن قلت) : أين مفعول تبتغوا؟ (قلت) : يجوز أن يكون مقدرا وهو: النساء، وأجود أن لا يقدر.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author says “spend” is not the apparent meaning of “seek”: the preposition bi- before wealth does not make wealth a direct object, so this analysis needlessly strains the text.
rows.anchor: مدلول تبتغوا ليس مدلول تخرجوا

rows.speaker: أبو سعيد
rows.claim: Abū Saʿīd and numerous early authorities hold that marriage may be contracted for a small or large amount of wealth.
rows.anchor: وهو قول: أبي سعيد، والحسن، وابن المسيب، وعطاء، والليث، وابن أبي ليلى، والثوري، والحسن بن صالح، والشافعي، وربيعة قالوا: يجوز النكاح

rows.speaker: أبو حنيفة
rows.claim: Abū Ḥanīfah, Abū Yūsuf, Zufar, and others set a ten-dirham minimum; Mālik sets a quarter dinar or three dirhams, while Abū Bakr al-Rāzī says one or two dirhams is not wealth.
rows.anchor: وهو قول: أبي حنيفة، وأبي يوسف، وزفر، والحسن، ومحمد بن زياد.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording “with your wealth” appears to exclude a non-monetary mahr; some permit service for a fixed period, while al-Shāfiʿī permits Quran instruction and Mālik, al-Layth, and the Hanafis reject it.
rows.anchor: وأجاز أن يكون تعليم سورة من القرآن الشافعي، ومنع من ذلك: مالك والليث، وأبو حنيفة، وأبو يوسف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Iḥṣān means chastity and self-protection; “chaste, not fornicators” is emphatic because chastity cannot coexist with fornication.
rows.anchor: والإحصان: العفة، وتحصين النفس عن الوقوع في الحرام.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās and others describe open, promiscuous fornication and secret one-to-one liaisons as two pre-Islamic forms; a khidn is a woman's secret lover, while safḥ evokes semen being poured.
rows.anchor: وكذلك متخذات الأخدان هن الزواني المتسترات

rows.speaker: مسروق والشعبي
rows.claim: They compare marrying an enslaved woman to eating carrion, blood, or pork: it is permissible only in necessity.
rows.anchor: وروي عن مسروق، والشعبي: أن نكاحها بمنزلة الميتة والدم ولحم الخنزير

rows.speaker: علي وأبو جعفر ومجاهد وابن المسيب وإبراهيم والحسن والزهري
rows.claim: They permit a man to marry an enslaved woman even when financially able to marry a free woman.
rows.anchor: وروي عن علي، وأبي جعفر، ومجاهد، وابن المسيب، وإبراهيم، والحسن، والزهري: أن له نكاحها، وإن كان موسرا.

rows.speaker: عطاء وجابر بن زيد
rows.claim: They permit marrying an enslaved woman when the man fears fornication, even if he already has a free wife; ʿAṭāʾ specifically permits taking her alongside the free wife.
rows.anchor: وروي عن عطاء، وجابر بن زيد: أنه يتزوجها إن خشي أن يزني بها، ولو كان تحته حرة.

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿūd says only an enslaved man may marry an enslaved woman when he already has a free wife.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن مسعود: لا يتزوجها عليها إلا المملوك.

rows.speaker: عمر وعلي وابن المسيب ومكحول
rows.claim: They prohibit marrying an enslaved woman while already having a free wife; the author says the Quran's inability condition makes this even clearer when a free wife is already present.
rows.anchor: وقال عمر، وعلي، وابن المسيب، ومكحول في آخرين: لا يتزوجها عليها.

rows.speaker: إبراهيم
rows.claim: Ibrāhīm permits an enslaved second wife if she bears the man a child; Ibn al-Musayyib permits it only with the free wife's consent and gives her two nights to the slave wife's one.
rows.anchor: وقال إبراهيم: يتزوج الأمة على الحرة إن كان له من الأمة ولد.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās restricts the man unable to afford a free wife to marrying at most one enslaved woman, although the apparent phrase allows four.
rows.anchor: وروي عن ابن عباس: أنه لا يتزوج من الإماء أكثر من واحدة، وإذا لم يكن شرطا

rows.speaker: أبو يوسف
rows.claim: Abū Yūsuf allows an enslaved woman owned by a non-Muslim to marry a Muslim with dislike; the author says the apparent wording either makes belief a condition or, if it does not, permits any unbelieving slave, although consensus bars non-scriptural unbelievers.
rows.anchor: وروي عن أبي يوسف: جواز ذلك على كراهة.

rows.speaker: طاوس
rows.claim: Ṭāwūs, ʿAṭāʾ, Mujāhid, and ʿAmr ibn Dīnār allow intercourse with a Magian slave by general Quranic wording, a position the author calls anomalous and abandoned; jurists require conversion first.
rows.anchor: وأما وطء المجوسية بملك اليمين فأجازه: طاوس، وعطاء، ومجاهد، وعمرو بن دينار.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Slave marriage is lower in status because the child follows its mother into slavery, the owner retains rights and use, and the woman remains subject to his comings and goings; accepting this entails diminished honor.
rows.anchor: لما فيه من اتباع الولد لأمه في الرق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Whoever among you is unable” begins a condition answered by fa; the implied command is to marry from what your right hands possess, though another parse treats the phrase as a relative pronoun with an omitted predicate.
rows.anchor: ومن مبتدأ، وظاهره أنه شرط. والفاء في: فمما ملكت فاء الجواب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent object of “is able” is ṭawlan; “to marry” may depend on an omitted preposition meaning resources to reach marriage or a mahr for it.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن مفعول يستطع هو طولا

rows.speaker: الفرزدق
rows.claim: Al-Farazdaq's line uses ṭāla with a direct object; this supports the Basran allowance for a verbal noun to govern an object and the interpretation that ṭawl means ability to attain marriage.
rows.anchor:
قالوا: ومنه قول الفرزدق:
إن الفرزدق صخرة عادية ...

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Abū ʿAlī makes ṭawlan the object of “is able” and the marriage infinitive the object of the verbal noun; other parses make the infinitive a substitute or direct object.
rows.anchor: ذهب أبو علي في التذكرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The most apparent parse makes mā in “from what your right hands possess” a relative noun, “from your slave girls” a circumstantial phrase, and the omitted command object an enslaved woman; min is partitive and “believing” modifies the girls.
rows.anchor: والأظهر أن المؤمنات صفة لفتياتكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other parses make min extra, place the object on slave girls or believing women, or read mā as a verbal noun meaning ownership; one especially strange reading rearranges the clause.
rows.anchor: وقيل: من في من ما زائدة، ومفعول ذلك الفعل هو ما من قوله: ما ملكت أيمانكم.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author rejects the reading attributed to al-Ṭabarī that “some of you are from others” supplies the subject of an omitted verb and requires reordered syntax, calling it ignorant and destructive of Quranic eloquence.
rows.anchor: ومن أغرب ما سطروه في كتب التفسير ونقلوه عن قول الطبري

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “God knows your faith” reassures that inward belief is God's knowledge; an enslaved woman's public profession suffices for marriage, even if she is mute or recently captured.
rows.anchor: فيكفي من الإيمان منهن إظهاره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The address “your faith” includes believing men and women, free and enslaved; its general form avoids excluding other believers by saying only “their faith.”
rows.anchor: والخطاب في بإيمانكم للمؤمنين ذكورهم وإناثهم، حرهم ورقهم، وانتظم الإيمان في هذا الخطاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some enslaved women surpass free women in faith and good works, and women may surpass men; this reassures about marrying slaves and teaches that faith outranks lineage and status.
rows.anchor: فوق حرة في الإيمان وفعل الخير، وامرأة تفوق رجلا في ذلك، وفي ذلك تأنيس لنكاح الإماء،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A Prophetic report denies any Arab or non-Arab superiority over the other except through piety.
rows.anchor: لا فضل لعربي على عجمي ولا عجمي على عربي إلا بالتقوى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The report makes piety the stated basis for distinction among Arabs and non-Arabs.
rows.anchor: لا فضل لعربي على عجمي ولا عجمي على عربي إلا بالتقوى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Some of you are from others” is a subject-predicate sentence that reassures people about slave marriage: free and enslaved believers share one origin and faith, undoing pre-Islamic stigma toward their children.
rows.anchor: الأحرار والأرقاء كلهم متواصلون متناسبون يرجعون إلى أصل واحد

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: ʿAlī's verse says people are equal in origin, their father Adam and mother Eve.
rows.anchor:
روي عن علي من قوله:
الناس من جهة التمثيل أكفاء ... أبوهم آدم والأم حواء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Marry them with their owners' permission” is permissive and means under the owners' guardianship; marriage here is the contract, and owners are called family because the slave returns to them in many legal matters.
rows.anchor: فانكحوهن بإذن أهلهن هذا أمر إباحة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording makes owner permission a condition of a slave woman's marriage, so a contract without it is invalid even if later approved; unauthorized male-slave marriages are disputed as suspended or invalid.
rows.anchor: فلو تزوجت بغير إذن السيد لم يصح النكاح

rows.speaker: ابن عمر
rows.claim: Ibn ʿUmar treated a male slave who married without his owner's permission as an adulterer and applied the penalty; ʿAṭāʾ says it violates the Sunna but is not zina, a view attributed to most early scholars.
rows.anchor: وكان ابن عمر يعده زانيا ويحده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “With their owners' permission” includes male and female owners; if permission means the contract itself, a female owner may perform it directly, though al-Shāfiʿī requires her to appoint another.
rows.anchor: وظاهر قوله: بإذن أهلهن أنه يشمل الملاك ذكورا وإناثا

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī says the verse requires owners' consent and supports Abū Ḥanīfah's position that female owners may contract the marriage themselves, since consent rather than their contract is specified.
rows.anchor: بإذن أهلهن، اشترط الإذن للموالي في نكاحهن، ويحتج به لقول أبي حنيفة

rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: The command to give enslaved women their mahr indicates that she owns it; Mālik says her master may not take it while leaving her without a trousseau.
rows.anchor: وهذا مذهب مالك، قال: ليس للسيد أن يأخذ مهر أمته ويدعها بلا جهاز.

rows.speaker: جمهور العلماء
rows.claim: Most scholars say the mahr must be paid to the owner, reasoning that the slave woman's assets belong to him; alternatives posit an omitted “owners” or carry forward the earlier owner-permission phrase.
rows.anchor: وجمهور العلماء: على أنه يجب دفعه للسيد دونها.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Wages” means dowries, not expenses, since maintenance follows consummation rather than the contract; “in a recognized manner” may mean prompt payment without harm, customary fair mahr, or may qualify the marriage itself.
rows.anchor: وكون الأجور يراد بها المهور هو الوجه، لأن النفقة تتعلق بالتمكين لا بالعقد.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās and others describe open, promiscuous fornication and secret one-to-one liaisons as two pre-Islamic forms; a khidn is a woman's secret lover, and the Quran bans both open and hidden indecencies.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: كان قوم يحرمون ما ظهر من الزنا ويستحلون ما خفي منه.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Chaste” is a circumstantial phrase likely governed by “pay them,” possibly meaning married rather than fornicating; another parse attaches it to “marry them” as chaste or Muslim.
rows.anchor: وانتصاب محصنات على الحال، والظاهر أن العامل فيه: وآتوهن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The punishment for an enslaved woman's fornication is flogging, not stoning, since stoning cannot be halved; the apparent half penalty is fifty lashes and half a year's exile if the free woman's penalty includes one year.
rows.anchor: ولا يمكن أن يراد الرجم، لأن الرجم لا يتنصف.

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī and a group of Successors hold that the penalty is fifty lashes and six months' exile; Ibn ʿAbbās and most scholars require fifty lashes without exile, depending on what “the punishment” refers to.
rows.anchor: وإلى هذا ذهب جماعة من التابعين، واختاره الطبري.

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: Most scholars hold that a master may not pardon an enslaved woman who incurs the penalty; al-Ḥasan allows pardon, and the verse does not specify who enforces it.
rows.anchor: والظاهر وجوب الحد من قوله: فعليهن، فلا يجوز العفو عن الأمة من السيد إذا زنت، وهو مذهب الجمهور.

rows.speaker: ابن شهاب
rows.claim: Ibn Shihāb says established practice lets owners punish enslaved men and women unless their case goes to the ruler; early reports cite the Prophet, Ibn ʿUmar, Anas, and the Anṣār.
rows.anchor: قال ابن شهاب: مضت السنة أن يحد الأمة والعبد في الزنا أهلوهم، إلا أن يرفع أمرهم إلى السلطان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet says that if one person's slave woman commits fornication, the owner should flog her the prescribed penalty; al-Thawrī and al-Awzāʿī agree.
rows.anchor: كقوله: «إذا زنت أمة أحدكم فليجلدها الحد»

rows.speaker: مالك والليث
rows.claim: Mālik and al-Layth permit the owner to impose penalties except amputation, which only the ruler may carry out; Abū Ḥanīfah reserves all penalties for the ruler.
rows.anchor: وقال مالك والليث: يحد السيد إلا في القطع، فلا يقطع إلا الإمام.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse requires the slave penalty if she was enslaved when the offense occurred, and consensus says she receives it even if freed before enforcement.
rows.anchor: وظاهر الآية يدل على وجوب الحد عليها في حال كونها أمة، فلو عتقت قبل أن يقام عليها الحد

rows.speaker: أهل الظاهر وداود
rows.claim: They say an enslaved woman who commits fornication a fourth time must also be sold; the apparent verse itself states only the ordinary penalty.
rows.anchor: وذهب أهل الظاهر منهم داود: إلى أنه يجب بيعها إذا زنت زنية رابعة.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī read “when they marry” actively, while most readers use the passive; passive plainly means marriage, and active can mean they protect themselves by marriage. The second fa introduces the conditional answer.
rows.anchor: ومن بناه للمفعول فهو ظاهر حدا في أنه أريد به التزوج

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “That” points back to marrying an enslaved woman when a man lacks means for a free believing wife.
rows.anchor: ذلك إشارة إلى نكاح عادم طول الحرة المؤمنة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, Ibn Jubayr, and others gloss ʿanat as fornication; its root is hardship, naming the hardship zina brings in this life and the next. Al-Mubarrid relates it to desire leading to sin and punishment.
rows.anchor: والعنت: هو الزنا. قاله: ابن عباس، ومجاهد، وابن جبير

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة والزجاج
rows.claim: They explain ʿanat as destruction; other groups gloss it as the legal penalty or the sin caused by overpowering desire.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو عبيدة والزجاج: العنت الهلاك.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent Quranic conditions for a free man to marry an enslaved woman are inability to afford a free believing wife, fear of fornication, and the enslaved woman being a believer.
rows.anchor: لا يجوز نكاح الحر الأمة إلا بثلاثة شروط

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, Ibn Jubayr, and al-Suddī take “if you are patient, it is better” as general patience: refraining from slave marriage avoids an enslaved child and customary loss of status.
rows.anchor: ابن عباس ومجاهد وابن جبير والسدي: وجهة الخيرية كونه لا يرق ولده

rows.speaker: أنس
rows.claim: Anas reports the Prophet recommending free women to whoever wants to meet God purified; another report says to marry equals and choose carefully for offspring.
rows.anchor:
وفي سنن ابن ماجه من حديث أنس قال:
سمعت رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم يقول:

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another interpretation makes patience mean abstaining from fornication rather than marrying enslaved women; that reading gently accepts slave marriage against Arab aversion. General patience also includes both restraints and merits the unlimited reward promised for patience.
rows.anchor: وقيل: المراد وإن تصبروا عن الزنا بنكاح الإماء خير لكم

rows.speaker: عطاء
rows.claim: ʿAṭāʾ says God explains what brings people near; al-Kalbī says the verse explains that patience in avoiding slave marriage is better.
rows.anchor: قال عطاء: يبين لكم ما يقربكم.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other interpretations take the explanation as permitted and forbidden rules, laws and religious interests, or a path to Paradise followed by prior communities.
rows.anchor: وقيل: شرائع دينكم، ومصالح أموركم.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author proposes an ellipsis in which the object of “make clear” is supplied by “guide you”: God makes clear to you the ways of those before you.
rows.anchor: ويجوز عندي أن يكون من باب الإعمال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If “ways of those before you” is literal, it may mean shared prohibitions, Abraham's path, the religion prescribed to Noah and later prophets, routes to Paradise, or righteous prophetic models; another view includes paths of truth and error.
rows.anchor: واختلفوا في قوله: سنن الذين من قبلكم، هل ذلك على ظاهره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The comparative reading says earlier peoples received guidance through messengers, books, and clarified rules as you do; it may also refer to shared commands despite differing rules or to obedience like theirs.
rows.anchor: والذين قالوا: إن ذلك على التشبيه قالوا: إن المعنى أن طرق الأمم السابقة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the syntax of “God wants,” al-Zamakhsharī reports the Kufan view, calls it weak, then returns to it; the author had presented Sībawayhi's analysis that the omitted object is “this clarification.”
rows.anchor: والتقدير: يريد الله هذا التبيين.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Desires are what the soul loves and inclines toward; because religious obligations restrain the self, yielding to desire is blameworthy, as in the description of those who abandon prayer and follow desires.
rows.anchor: والشهوات جمع شهوة، وهي ما يغلب على النفس محبته وهواه.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mujāhid identifies the followers of desires as fornicators; al-Suddī says Jews and Christians or Jews who wanted Muslims to copy their marriage to paternal half-sisters.
rows.anchor: ومتبعو الشهوات هنا هم الزناة قاله: مجاهد. أو اليهود والنصارى قاله: السدي.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage also says Magians permitted paternal half-sisters and nieces, then objected when Muslims prohibited those but permitted cousins.
rows.anchor: أو المجوس كانوا يحلون نكاح الأخوات من الأب، ونكاح بنات الأخ، وبنات الأخت

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd takes “followers of desires” to mean all who follow any desire; al-Ṭabarī prefers this broader interpretation.
rows.anchor: أو متبعو كل شهوة قاله: ابن زيد، ورجحه الطبري.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase is generally worded; “incline” means turning from truth into injustice and leaving the straight path, contrasting God's will with that of desire-followers.
rows.anchor: وإن كان مطلقا فالمراد هنا الميل عن الحق، وهو الجور والخروج عن قصد السبيل.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The emphatic infinitive “a great inclination” heightens the warning: motives for wrongdoing vary, but the hardest to remedy is unbelief.
rows.anchor: وأكد فعل الميل بالمصدر على سبيل المبالغة، لم يكتف حتى وصفه بالعظم.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most readers address the audience with “that you incline”; another reading uses third person for desire-followers. Most read maylan with a silent yāʾ; al-Ḥasan opens it.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: أن تميلوا بتاء الخطاب. وقرىء: بالياء على الغيبة.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most readers pronounce maylan with a silent yāʾ, while al-Ḥasan opens it.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: ميلا بسكون الياء. وقرأ الحسن:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The segment completes the reading note with al-Ḥasan's vocalization, then contrasts the stable divine will in a nominal sentence with the renewed intent of desire-followers in a verbal one.
rows.anchor: بفتحها، وجاءت الجملة الأولى اسمية، والثانية فعلية لإظهار تأكيد الجملة الأولى

rows.speaker: الراغب
rows.claim: Al-Rāghib allows the waw to introduce a circumstantial clause, meaning God wills repentance while people desire to turn away.
rows.anchor: وأجاز الراغب أن تكون الواو للحال لا للعطف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author rejects the circumstantial reading: God's will to grant repentance is not conditional on others' desire to deviate, and a directly waw-linked imperfect is an anomalous construction.
rows.anchor: وهذا ليس بجيد، لأن إرادته تعالى التوبة علينا ليست مقيدة بإرادة غيره الميل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The unstated object of “God wants to lighten for you” has several proposed senses: concessions such as slave marriage, clarified rules, removal of earlier burdens, reward for obligations, or pardon for ignorant sins.
rows.anchor: يريد الله أن يخفف عنكم لم يذكر متعلق التخفيف، وفي ذلك أقوال:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Treating the clause as circumstantial from “God wants to grant you repentance” is grammatically weak because a separate coordinated clause intervenes and the verb takes an explicit subject; the author prefers an independent sentence, like the promise of ease.
rows.anchor: وأعربوا هذه الجملة حالا من قوله: والله يريد أن يتوب عليكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author prefers taking “God wants to lighten for you” as an independent sentence with no syntactic role, parallel to God's statement that He wants ease for people.
rows.anchor: والأحسن أن تكون الجملة مستأنفة، فلا موضع لها من الإعراب.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The definite article in “the indecency” may use a whole-class form for emphasis though only one kind is intended, unless it conventionally means zina; “afflict them,” “a way,” and “leave them” are also interpreted narrowly as rebuke or penalty and abandonment.
rows.anchor: التجوز بإطلاق اسم الكل على البعض في قوله: يأتين الفاحشة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The text attributes actions to something other than their actual agent in “until death takes them” and “when death comes to one of them.”
rows.anchor: وإسناد الفعل إلى غير فاعله في قوله: حتى يتوفاهن الموت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage uses altered-word paronomasia in “if the two repent, God is ever accepting repentance,” in nursing/breastfeeding, and in protected women/being protected.
rows.anchor: والتجنيس المغاير في: فإن تابا إن الله كان توابا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author catalogs repeated words across the passage, including repentance, wives, mothers, “except what has passed,” believers, mahr, faith, and God's will; he also notes future forms used for past events.
rows.anchor: والتكرار في: اسم الله في مواضع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Expressions imply linked rules: reluctance hints consensual inheritance transfer; the ban on coercing wives allows restraint for their benefit; the prohibition on fathers' wives recalls pre-Islamic practice; permission points to prior bans; slave-marriage conditions and human weakness point to desire.
rows.anchor: والإشارة والإيماء في قوله: كرها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mentioning a qinṭār of dowry magnifies the matter and forcefully deters a husband from reclaiming it.
rows.anchor: والمبالغة في تفخيم الأمر وتأكيده في قوله: وآتيتم إحداهن قنطارا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author identifies metaphors in taking a solemn covenant, calling an obligation God's book, and treating chastity as a fortress, giving concrete images to abstract bonds and restraint.
rows.anchor: استعار الأخذ للوثوق بالميثاق والتمسك به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Metaphors include chastity as a fortress, safḥ as semen poured out, mahr as wages, ṭawl as means to an end, following desires as movement from truth, and easing obligations as reducing weight.
rows.anchor: واستعار لكثرة الزنا السفح وهو صب الماء في الأنهار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling control or marriage of women “inheritance” names its result under pre-Islamic custom; calling humans weak names their likely outcome or origin.
rows.anchor: تسمية الشيء بما يؤول إليه في قوله: أن ترثوا النساء كرها، سمي تزويج النساء أو منعهن للأزواج إرثا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “You may dislike something while God places much good in it” is an antithesis between disliking and beneficial outcome.
rows.anchor: والطباق المعنوي في قوله: وعسى أن تكرهوا شيئا ويجعل الله فيه خيرا كثيرا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He calls “forbidden to you” followed by “made lawful” verbal antithesis; “chaste, not fornicators” also opposes guarding sexuality to making it freely available.
rows.anchor: وفي قوله: والمحصنات من النساء، أي حرام عليكم ثم قال: وأحل لكم.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Those you have entered upon” excludes unconsummated marriages; “stepdaughters in your care” and “of women” add qualifications. The statements about faith and shared origin are parenthetical, with omissions elsewhere.
rows.anchor: والاحتراس في قوله: اللاتي دخلتم بهن احترز من اللاتي لم يدخل بهن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Following desires and inclination are metaphors for yielding to the soul and leaving the truth; the source also compares easing obligations to reducing physical weight.
rows.anchor: وفي قوله: يتبعون الشهوات استعار الاتباع والميل اللذين هما حقيقة في الإجرام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This segment reproduces Quranic verses 6:36–52 without commentary.
rows.anchor: إنما يستجيب الذين يسمعون والموتى يبعثهم الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tadarruʿ means humble abasement; an anonymous poet's line about being weak when sued illustrates a submissive and frail person.
rows.anchor: التضرع: تفعل من الضراعة وهي الذلة

rows.speaker: ابن الرقاع
rows.claim: Ibn al-Riqāʿ's poem uses ṣadaf for turning away; it may also mean a camel's hoof turning outward or a shell, and another poem evokes a pearl's turning within its shell.
rows.anchor: قال ابن الرقاع: إذا ذكرن حديثا قلن أحسنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A khizāna is a store protecting its contents; a Prophetic report pictures animals' udders as stored food, and a poem describes a guarded tongue.
rows.anchor: الخزانة ما يحفظ فيه الشيء مخافة أن ينال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṭard means expulsion accompanied by humiliation; ṭarīd means an expelled person, and the author notes tribal names derived from these terms.
rows.anchor: الطرد الإبعاد بإهانة والطريد المطرود

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Only those who hear respond” means those who listen receptively and attentively; istajāba implies accepting an invitation, unlike ajāba, which can answer against it.
rows.anchor: إنما يستجيب للإيمان الذين يسمعون سماع قبول وإصغاء

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī says those the Prophet hopes will believe are like the dead, who do not hear, citing the Quran's statement that he cannot make the dead hear.
rows.anchor: قال الزمخشري يعني أن الذين تحرص على أن يصدقوك بمنزلة الموتى

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyyah reads this as consolation: do not concern yourself with those who turn away; believers understand signs and accept proofs, and “hearing” summarizes the path to knowing prophethood and miracles.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عطية هذا من النمط المتقدم في التسلية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “The dead God will raise” is an independent statement about literal resurrection and judgment of everyone; its generality follows the preceding universal statement and threatens those who do not respond.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن الموت هنا والبعث حقيقة وذلك إخبار من الله تعالى

rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: Commentators broadly take “the dead” as unbelievers metaphorically: as a corpse lacks spirit, the unbeliever lacks reason, showing ignorance of God, disobedience, and rejection of prophetic signs; reason relates to soul as spirit to body.
rows.anchor: وتظافرت أقوال المفسرين أن قوله والموتى يراد به الكفار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The general “no creature on earth” already includes birds; naming birds afterward specifies part after whole and highlights their extraordinary movement as evidence of divine power.
rows.anchor: فهي عامة تشمل كل ما يدب فيندرج فيها الطائر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Birds are singled out because movement through subtle air is a clearer sign of power than movement over dense ground; God alone holds birds aloft in the sky.
rows.anchor: والهواء جسم لطيف لا يمكن عادة تصرف الأجرام الكثيفة فيها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “On earth” generalizes location and includes land and sea; “with its two wings” reinforces flight and rules out a figurative reading of bird as a person's deeds.
rows.anchor: ويطير بجناحيه تأكيد لقوله ولا طائر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author compares naming birds after all creatures with naming Gabriel and Michael after angels, and notes “bird” can metaphorically mean a person's deeds.
rows.anchor: ألا ترى إلى استعارة الطائر للعمل في قوله: وكل إنسان ألزمناه طائره في عنقه
